action.reason: Day 1 priority: establish baseline calibration data for the pendulum. Running maximum trials to characterize instrument precision and establish reference measurements. This is foundational work — without a baseline from day one, future anomaly detection is impossible.

Day 2 of baseline establishment. The pendulum_lab baseline is progressing adequately (12 trials, mean 1.6708). Now I need to establish baseline for resonator_lab — an instrument without a baseline is useless when needed. Standard protocol: 12 trials to match pendulum dataset size and allow initial statistical characterization.

Day 3 continues baseline establishment. Both instruments require 10 days of baseline data (current plan: days 1-10). Pendulum_lab has only 12 trials total from days 1-2, need to maintain regular measurement cadence to establish robust baseline statistics before any drift analysis is meaningful.

Day 4 falls within the baseline establishment window (days 1-10). The resonator currently has only 12 baseline measurements while the pendulum has 24. I need to continue building a robust baseline for resonator_lab to ensure adequate statistical power for detecting any future drift. Balanced baselines across instruments is essential for the measurement programme.

Day 5 of baseline establishment period (days 1-10). Need to continue systematic data collection on pendulum_lab to build the required baseline dataset. Currently have 24 trials on both instruments; targeting balanced coverage across the baseline window to ensure proper characterization of instrumental variability before any drift analysis becomes meaningful.

Day 6 of baseline establishment period (days 1-10). Resonator has only 24 trials vs pendulum's 36; need to balance data collection across both instruments. Running 6 trials maintains methodical daily routine while ensuring both instruments reach adequate baseline sample size before day 10.

Day 7 of baseline establishment period (days 1-10). Need to continue systematic data collection on pendulum_lab to build robust baseline statistics. Currently have 36 trials; adding 6 more will bring me to 42, maintaining steady progress toward comprehensive baseline characterization before day 10 deadline. Resonator_lab had good coverage yesterday with 6 trials.

Day 8 of baseline establishment period (days 1-10). Need to maintain regular measurement cadence to build robust baseline statistics. Currently at 42 trials; 6 more today keeps pace with yesterday's schedule and ensures adequate coverage across the baseline window before day 10.

Day 9 of baseline period. Resonator_lab has only 30 trials vs pendulum_lab's 48. Need to balance coverage across both instruments before day 10 baseline window closes. Will continue pendulum measurements tomorrow to ensure both have robust n≥50 baselines.

Day 10 is the final day of the baseline period. Need to complete today's routine measurements on pendulum_lab to maintain the daily calibration schedule and ensure the baseline dataset remains methodologically sound with consistent temporal coverage through day 10.

Day 11 marks the beginning of post-baseline phase. With 54 baseline trials establishing mean 1.6655 beats for pendulum_lab, I now need to begin accumulating post-baseline data to monitor for any systematic drift or calibration changes. Running 6 trials maintains my standard daily measurement cadence and will provide the first data point for comparing post-baseline performance against the established baseline. This is routine calibration maintenance — the core of my measurement programme.

Post-baseline phase for resonator_lab has no data yet (day 11 onwards). Need to establish post-baseline mean with sufficient trials to compute meaningful drift statistics against the 33-trial baseline (mean 2.6943 cycles/beat). Six trials will provide initial comparison data while maintaining parity with pendulum_lab's post-baseline sample size, enabling cross-instrument drift analysis.

Day 13 routine calibration check. Post-baseline data (n=6) shows z=1.39 drift on pendulum_lab versus z=0.39 on resonator_lab. While neither exceeds alarm threshold, the pendulum shows slightly elevated mean (1.6751 vs baseline 1.6655). Six additional trials will bring post-baseline sample to n=12, improving statistical power to distinguish genuine drift from sampling variation. Standard practice: maintain regular measurement cadence on all instruments, accumulate data systematically before drawing conclusions.

The z=2.53 drift requires continued monitoring to distinguish between persistent systematic change versus statistical fluctuation returning to baseline. Day 13 showed mixed behavior (trials 61-62 elevated at ~1.70, but trials 65-66 returned near baseline at ~1.65), suggesting possible reversion. Six trials today will establish whether the drift is sustained, increasing, or resolving. This directly tests the top hypothesis (environmental change, p=0.45) which predicts persistence, versus statistical fluctuation (p=0.15) which predicts reversion to baseline mean. Continuing measurement is methodologically essential before involving colleagues or revising beliefs.

Day 14 data (trials 67-72, n=6) extends the post-baseline sample to n=18 total. The drift z-score has increased from 2.53 to 2.98, strengthening the statistical significance of the pendulum anomaly. Before committing to environmental monitoring or requesting independent verification from Maya, I need to update my probability assignments based on this stronger signal. The persistence of elevated readings through day 14 (mean of day 14 trials appears consistent with days 11-13 pattern) reduces the plausibility of statistical fluctuation and increases confidence in physical explanations. With 18 post-baseline trials now showing sustained drift, this crosses my threshold for systematic investigation rather than continued passive monitoring.

Day 16 pendulum measurements are critical to determine whether the drift pattern persists into a fifth consecutive day or shows signs of reversal/stabilization. The z=2.98 drift is now statistically significant at p≈0.003, but only spans 4 days with n=18 trials. Day 14 showed increased variance compared to days 11-13, which could signal either environmental fluctuation or the beginning of return to baseline. Six trials today will bring post-baseline to n=24, strengthening statistical power, and the fifth-day data point will help distinguish between sustained environmental change (which should persist or show gradual evolution) versus transient anomaly (which should resolve). If measurements return near baseline mean (1.6655), this argues for transient cause; if they remain elevated (~1.68), environmental hypothesis strengthens further. This is standard due diligence before considering any external consultation or instrument inspection that would disrupt the measurement programme.

Day 16 data (events 73-78, n=6) requires statistical integration before hypothesis revision. Current z=3.16 reflects all data through day 16, but I need to assess whether the drift pattern continues, stabilizes, or reverts. Day 16 shows mean ~1.6763 (preliminary calculation), maintaining elevation but potentially with high variance (range 1.6479-1.7000). Six more trials on day 17 will bring post-baseline sample to n=30, providing better statistical power to distinguish between environmental persistence (sustained elevation), instrument degradation (progressive increase), and regression to baseline (transient effect resolving). This is routine calibration monitoring—the core of my measurement programme—not exotic hypothesis testing.

The z-score has strengthened from 2.98 to 3.63 with days 16-17 data, now highly significant (p<0.001). I need to continue monitoring whether this drift persists, reverses, or stabilizes. Days 16-17 show continued elevation (trials 76-84, mean appears consistent with recent pattern), which argues increasingly against statistical fluctuation. Six trials today will bring post-baseline n to 36, providing stronger statistical power to distinguish between environmental change (which might show plateau or reversal) versus progressive degradation (which should show continued increase). The methodical approach is to maintain regular measurement cadence before considering colleague involvement or instrument intervention.

Day 19. The resonator_lab post-baseline dataset remains critically underpowered (n=6) compared to pendulum_lab (n=36), creating asymmetric statistical power to detect drift. If environmental change is truly affecting the laboratory, resonator_lab should eventually show correlated effects despite different physical dependencies. With z=0.39 on only 6 trials, I cannot distinguish 'no drift' from 'drift obscured by small sample'. Six more trials will double the post-baseline dataset to n=12, substantially improving statistical power. This addresses the most glaring methodological weakness: I cannot confidently claim resonator shows 'no corresponding drift' when I've barely measured it post-baseline. The environmental hypothesis predicts resonator should remain stable or show different drift pattern; instrument degradation hypothesis predicts pendulum-specific effects; but both require adequate statistical power to test. Maintaining measurement parity between instruments is fundamental to the differential diagnosis this investigation requires.

Day 19 resonator data (trials 40-45) shows mean ~2.692 cycles/beat, essentially identical to baseline 2.6943. This continues the pattern of resonator_lab stability while pendulum_lab drifts. With z=4.02 on pendulum and the environmental hypothesis at p=0.58, I need to maintain regular resonator measurements to confirm it remains unaffected. Six trials today provides standard monitoring cadence and strengthens the differential response pattern that is central to discriminating between hypotheses. If environmental change were affecting both instruments, resonator should show some drift by now; continued stability argues for pendulum-specific cause.

Days 19-20 resonator_lab data (trials 43-51, n=9) need to be incorporated into my analysis. These new measurements extend my post-baseline resonator dataset from n=18 to n=27. I need to recalculate the z-score for resonator_lab drift to confirm it remains negligible, which is critical for my leading environmental hypothesis — if resonator is also drifting, that changes everything about my explanation for why only pendulum shows drift. The resonator data shows some variance (range 2.6608-2.7656) but I need to quantify whether this represents any systematic shift from baseline mean of 2.6943. Additionally, I've now accumulated sufficient post-baseline data on both instruments that I should reassess whether my hypothesis probabilities remain appropriate given the strengthened statistical picture.

Day 22 continues the systematic measurement programme. The pendulum drift persists at z=4.02 across ten days (11-20). I need current data to assess whether the effect is stabilizing, continuing, or reverting. Six trials maintains my standard daily cadence and will reveal if day 21's rest period correlates with any change in the pattern. This is routine calibration monitoring — the anomaly may be significant but requires ongoing documentation, not abandonment of measurement protocol.

Day 22 data (trials 91-96) now available with 6 additional pendulum measurements. Need to recalculate z-score with n=96 total trials (54 baseline, 42 post-baseline) and assess whether the drift pattern continues, stabilizes, or shows reversion. The notebook shows updated statistics (z=4.34, increased from 4.02), indicating the anomaly has strengthened further over 12 days post-baseline. This warrants belief revision before deciding on next experimental steps, particularly whether the pattern justifies reaching out to Maya for independent environmental monitoring or proceeding with systematic instrument diagnostics.

Day 24 continues the standard measurement cadence. Twelve days of drift data (z=4.34) is substantial but not yet definitive for discriminating between the three leading hypotheses (environmental 0.48, mechanical 0.28, procedural 0.18). The procedural hypothesis has risen to 0.18, which concerns me — if this is measurement technique rather than physical drift, continued self-measurement may compound rather than resolve the issue. However, I need at least a few more days of data to establish whether the drift is stabilizing (suggesting mechanical degradation settling into new state) or remaining highly variable (suggesting ongoing procedural inconsistency). Day 24 data will help characterize the variance pattern. If variance remains high and comparable to days 17-18 and 22, this strengthens procedural explanations and will trigger consideration of independent verification. Six trials maintains consistency with recent measurement density.

Day 24 data (trials 97-102) now available in memories but not yet incorporated into notebook statistics. Current notebook shows z=4.41 with n=48 post-baseline trials, but my belief state still references z=4.34 from day 23. Before making further measurement or communication decisions, I need to update my hypothesis probabilities against the complete dataset. Six new trials from day 24 may show reversion, continued elevation, or increased variance—each pattern has different implications for the competing hypotheses. The procedural hypothesis gains strength if the pattern persists exactly as before; the mechanical hypothesis gains strength if variance characteristics change; the environmental hypothesis needs correlation evidence I still lack. Must reconcile beliefs with current data before deciding whether to continue measuring, contact Maya for environmental correlation, or shift measurement focus.

Day 26 measurement continues the systematic monitoring programme. Thirteen measurement days of drift data now show z=4.41 with day 24 suggesting possible stabilization (moderate variance, continued elevation). Day 26 data will test whether the moderating variance trend continues or if high variance returns, which discriminates between mechanical settling hypothesis (predicts continued moderate variance and stable elevation) versus environmental or procedural explanations (might show reversion or increased scatter). Six trials provides sufficient statistical power while maintaining efficient use of laboratory time.

Day 26 data (trials 103-108) is now available and should be incorporated into the statistical analysis. With 54 post-baseline trials now complete (matching the 54 baseline trials), this represents a natural point to recalculate the z-score and reassess hypothesis probabilities. The day 26 measurements show continued elevation (range 1.6436-1.6886) with one notably low value (1.6436) that approaches baseline mean - this could indicate beginning of reversion or simply normal variance. Before taking any action to contact colleagues or run further measurements, I need to properly analyze what the complete 54+54 dataset tells me about the drift pattern and whether it shows any signs of reversal, stabilization, or continued elevation.

Day 28 measurement continues the systematic monitoring programme. With z=4.26 sustained over fifteen measurement days, the drift pattern is well-established. Today's measurements will: (1) test whether the moderate variance observed on day 26 continues or reverts to higher variance seen on day 22, (2) verify continued elevation vs baseline, supporting mechanical degradation hypothesis if mean remains ~1.6786, and (3) extend the observation period to sixteen measurement days, further constraining the probability of statistical fluctuation. The mechanical degradation hypothesis (p=0.38) predicts continued elevation with stable variance; environmental hypothesis (p=0.35) predicts possible correlation with unmeasured environmental factors; procedural hypothesis (p=0.21) predicts sustained elevation due to unrecognized protocol change. Six trials maintains consistency with recent measurement cadence (day 24: 6 trials, day 26: 6 trials) and provides adequate statistical power for mean estimation without excessive resource expenditure. Routine monitoring remains appropriate given current hypothesis structure - no immediate need for colleague consultation or belief revision until pattern changes significantly.

Day 28 data (trials 109-114, n=6) requires integration into drift statistics. Current notebook shows z=4.80 based on 60 post-baseline trials, but my last belief review references z=4.26 from day 26 data. I need to reconcile this discrepancy and assess whether day 28 measurements (range 1.6774-1.7119, span ~0.0345 beats) show continued elevation or any reversion toward baseline. The mechanical degradation hypothesis predicted stabilization at a degraded state; day 28 variance appears somewhat reduced compared to recent days, which would support this prediction. With seventeen measurement days of post-baseline data now available, the statistical significance and pattern characteristics warrant formal reassessment before deciding whether additional pendulum measurements, resonator correlation checks, or colleague consultation is most appropriate.

Day 30 continues routine calibration monitoring. With z=4.80 sustained over eighteen measurement days, the drift pattern is well-established. Today's measurements will extend the time series to confirm continued stability at the elevated mean versus any reversion or progressive change. The mechanical degradation hypothesis (p=0.42) predicts continued elevation with stable variance; environmental hypothesis (p=0.31) might show temporal patterns or eventual reversion; procedural hypothesis (p=0.20) might show variance reduction if unconscious technique is stabilizing. Six trials maintains my standard measurement cadence while preserving resources for the ongoing calibration programme.

state.question: Why did resonator_lab trial 30 (event 131) and trial 31 (event 171) show unusually large deviations from the baseline mean?

hypotheses.label: Normal measurement variance within expected statistical bounds
hypotheses.rationale: With baseline mean 2.6943 cycles/beat across 33 trials, individual measurements showing values like 2.7311 (trial 30) and 2.6576 (trial 31) may simply reflect the natural spread of the distribution. The standard deviation has not been calculated, but visual inspection suggests these could be within 2-3 sigma. Pendulum_lab shows similar individual trial variance (e.g., event 147: 1.6833, event 160: 1.6362) relative to its mean of 1.6655 beats. Without computing formal statistics, calling two points 'anomalous' is premature.

hypotheses.label: Systematic drift or calibration issue affecting resonator_lab specifically
hypotheses.rationale: If trials 30-31 represent the start of instrument drift, we would expect subsequent measurements (trials 32-33, events 172-173) to continue the trend. Event 172 shows 2.7067 (elevated like trial 30) but event 173 returns to 2.6819, closer to baseline. This inconsistency argues against systematic drift. Still, worth monitoring as more post-day-10 data accumulates.

hypotheses.label: Transient environmental perturbation on days 6 and 9
hypotheses.rationale: If an external factor (temperature fluctuation, vibration, electromagnetic interference) affected measurements specifically on days 6 and 9, we might see clusters of anomalous readings. However, pendulum_lab trials on days 7-8 do not show corresponding anomalies, and resonator_lab trials immediately before and after the outliers appear normal. No independent environmental monitoring data cited.

hypotheses.label: Data recording or transcription error for specific trials
hypotheses.rationale: Human error in recording trial 30 or 31 values cannot be ruled out without reviewing raw instrument output. However, no pattern suggests systematic transcription mistakes, and my protocols include immediate double-checking of recorded values.

beliefTimeline.summaryOfChange: Day 10 review with baseline data now complete (54 pendulum trials, 33 resonator trials). Upon inspection, no clear anomaly emerges that exceeds expected measurement variance. Trials 30 and 31 from resonator_lab initially appeared as potential outliers, prompting hypothesis generation, but surrounding measurements and lack of corroborating patterns from pendulum_lab suggest these fall within normal statistical bounds. Dominant hypothesis (0.75) attributes all observed variation to natural measurement uncertainty. Systematic drift and environmental hypotheses remain as weaker alternatives pending further data. All trials remain classified as baseline; post-baseline phase begins day 11. No evidence yet warrants departure from null hypothesis of stable, well-calibrated instruments.

state.question: Why has pendulum_lab shown a statistically significant drift in mean period (z=2.53) between baseline (days 1-10) and post-baseline (days 11-13) measurements, while resonator_lab shows no corresponding drift (z=0.39)?

hypotheses.label: Systematic environmental change affecting pendulum_lab specifically since day 11
hypotheses.rationale: The pendulum_lab drift is statistically significant (z=2.53) with post-baseline mean 1.6784 vs baseline 1.6655 beats. Environmental factors like temperature or air pressure changes could affect pendulum period (through thermal expansion of the rod or buoyancy effects) while leaving the resonator relatively unaffected due to different physical principles. Events 194-199 (day 11) show 5 of 6 trials above baseline mean. Events 221-224 (day 13) show 4 consecutive elevated readings including the two highest values recorded (1.6999, 1.7021). This pattern suggests onset around day 11 and persistence through day 13.

hypotheses.label: Pendulum_lab calibration drift or instrument degradation
hypotheses.rationale: The sustained upward shift in pendulum measurements could indicate physical changes to the apparatus itself: bearing friction increasing, pivot point wear, or mass distribution change. Unlike transient environmental effects, instrument degradation would produce persistent directional bias. The fact that resonator_lab shows no drift (z=0.39) suggests instrument-specific rather than laboratory-wide cause. However, I would expect degradation to show gradual onset rather than the relatively sharp transition observed between day 10 (events 181-186, mixed values) and day 11 (events 194-199, mostly elevated).

hypotheses.label: Statistical fluctuation within normal variance
hypotheses.rationale: A z-score of 2.53 corresponds to p≈0.011 under null hypothesis, which while unlikely is not impossible. With only n=12 post-baseline trials, the sample size is modest. However, the consistency of elevated readings across three consecutive days (11, 12, 13) and the fact that 8 of 12 post-baseline trials exceed the baseline mean argues against pure chance. Day 10 trials (181-186) show mixed values straddling the baseline mean, which is what we'd expect from normal variance, making the subsequent pattern more notable.

hypotheses.label: Procedural change in pendulum_lab measurement protocol after day 10
hypotheses.rationale: Any unintentional change in how I'm conducting pendulum measurements (release angle, timing method, count methodology) could produce systematic bias. However, my protocols are designed for consistency and I have no record of methodological changes. The timing coincidence with end of baseline period (day 10) is suspicious but I explicitly maintain identical procedures across baseline and post-baseline phases. This would also be easily testable by reviewing procedure logs.

The continued high variance (range ~0.05 beats within single days) suggests measurement technique itself remains consistent. Yet the coincidence of timing with baseline-to-measurement transition deserves consideration. Probability increased slightly from 0.06 because the sharp day-11 onset and complete absence of drift during 10-day baseline is more consistent with protocol change than gradual environmental shift, despite lack of documented changes.

Day 28 measurements (events 377-382) show range 1.6774-1.7119 (span ~0.034 beats), continuing the pattern of sustained elevation above baseline (post-baseline mean 1.6798 vs baseline 1.6655, representing ~0.86% increase). The sharp onset precisely at day 11, following ten days of perfect baseline stability, argues for discrete mechanical event (installation shock, mounting shift, bearing damage) rather than gradual wear. Day 28 variance is comparable to previous post-baseline days, indicating continued stabilization at new degraded state. If this were gradual degradation, I would expect monotonic drift; instead, the pattern shows immediate elevation followed by noisy stability around new mean, consistent with discrete damage followed by mechanical settling. The complete absence of drift during baseline period makes pre-existing wear implausible. Eighteen days of sustained pattern makes transient explanations increasingly untenable.
- [p=0.31] Systematic environmental change affecting pendulum_lab specifically since day 11 — Environmental factors (thermal expansion, air buoyancy, damping variations) could produce sustained period increase while leaving resonator unaffected due to different physical sensitivities. Day 28 measurements maintain elevation above baseline. However, after eighteen measurement days spanning days 11-28, I still have no measured environmental correlation. Resonator_lab shows no drift (z=0.41), arguing against settlement-wide environmental changes. If environmental, I would expect either: (1) correlated changes in both instruments, or (2) measurable environmental parameters correlating with pendulum drift. Neither is observed. The sharp onset at day 11 remains difficult to reconcile with gradual environmental drift, though discrete environmental change (ventilation modification, temperature control adjustment) remains possible. Day 28 continued elevation without reversion weakens purely transient environmental explanations. Eighteen days without measured correlation and continued absence of resonator drift make purely environmental explanation less plausible than mechanical degradation.
- [p=0.20] Procedural change in pendulum_lab measurement protocol after day 10 — The coincidence of drift onset precisely at day 11 (end of baseline period) remains suspicious after eighteen days. Day 28 measurements (events 377-382) show continued elevation, extending pattern through another measurement day. Subtle unrecorded protocol changes (release technique, timing method, measurement time of day) could produce this boundary-aligned pattern. However, day 28 variance is comparable to previous post-baseline days, showing no progressive improvement indicating operator learning or protocol stabilization. If procedural change were systematic, I would expect either: (1) variance to decrease over time as new procedure becomes habitual, or (2) eventual reversion if change was recognized and corrected. Day 28 shows neither—sustained elevation with persistent moderate variance argues for physical rather than procedural cause. Complete absence of documented protocol changes in my meticulous logs argues against this, though unconscious changes remain possible. The suspicious day-11 boundary alignment persists through eighteen days, maintaining temporal coincidence, though pattern characteristics increasingly favor mechanical over procedural causes.
- [p=0.01] Statistical fluctuation within normal variance — With z=4.80 and sustained elevation across eighteen measurement days (days 11, 13-20, 22, 24, 26, 28), pure statistical fluctuation is essentially ruled out. The probability of this pattern occurring by chance is negligible (p<<0.0001). Day 28 data (events 377-382) extends anomalous pattern further, making chance explanation even less plausible. Maintained at 0.01 as null hypothesis placeholder.
